topic: NPCI Introduces MDR on UPI Transactions

subtopics.title: MDR framework and rates
subtopics.summary: NPCI has introduced a Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) framework for eligible person-to-merchant (P2M) UPI transactions, effective from 15 October 2026. The main rate is 0.4 per cent of value for the mid-value slab. The zero-MDR policy introduced in 2020 had exempted merchants from paying any fee for UPI and RuPay transactions.
facts: Framework covers eligible P2M UPI transactions above ₹2,000
New framework comes into effect from 15 October 2026
MDR of 0.40% of value applies to the mid-value slab
High-value transactions of ₹75,000 and above are capped at ₹300 per transaction
Zero-MDR policy for UPI and RuPay was introduced in 2020
Zero-MDR policy aimed to encourage digital adoption among small businesses and informal sectors
MDR is a fee for processing a digital payment, borne by the merchant

subtopics.title: Exemptions, caps and special categories
subtopics.summary: Several categories of UPI payments are exempt from MDR, including person-to-person (P2P) transactions and P2M payments up to ₹2,000. Small merchants receiving up to ₹1 lakh per month through UPI QR codes under the P2PM category also remain exempt. Sector-specific payments and capital-market payments follow separate charging structures.
facts: P2P UPI transactions are not subject to MDR
P2M UPI payments up to ₹2,000 are exempt, including through RuPay debit cards
Transactions involving small vendors are exempt
Small merchants receiving up to ₹1 lakh per month via UPI QR codes (P2PM) remain exempt
Railways, telecom, insurance, fuel and agricultural inputs pay a flat MDR of ₹5 per transaction above ₹2,000
Mutual funds, securities, stock brokers and stock dealers attract a reduced MDR of 0.02%
Capital-market payments are subject to a ₹300 cap
Lower capital-market rate is intended to encourage digital payments in formal financial markets

subtopics.title: Why MDR was introduced
subtopics.summary: The booklet lists several reasons for the MDR framework, centred on the financial sustainability of UPI. Revenue from the framework can fund infrastructure, cybersecurity and innovation. The framework also keeps P2P and low-value merchant payments free to protect consumers.
facts: UPI requires continuous investment in payment infrastructure and technology
Growing digital payments need stronger systems to prevent fraud and cyber threats
A revenue mechanism can support continued operation and expansion of UPI
Revenue can support technological improvements and new payment solutions
Framework keeps P2P payments and low-value merchant payments free
Eligible small merchants continue to receive zero-MDR benefits
A self-funded payment ecosystem can reduce dependence on continued public funding
Small merchants and ordinary users need protection from additional costs

subtopics.title: MDR, UPI and NPCI basics
subtopics.summary: MDR is a fee charged on digital payment transactions and borne by the merchant, and it is not a tax collected by the government. UPI is a real-time, 24/7 payment system that is accepted in 11 countries. NPCI was established in 2008 as a Section 8 company under the Companies Act 2013.
facts: MDR is distributed among banks, payment service providers and other relevant participants
MDR is not a tax collected by the government
MDR revenue remains within the payment ecosystem
UPI is a real-time, 24/7, instant and interoperable payment system
UPI is the world's largest retail fast payment system by transaction volume
UPI is accepted in 11 countries, including Greece, Singapore, France and Qatar
NPCI was established in 2008 as a Section 8 company under the Companies Act 2013
NPCI was set up as an initiative of the RBI and the Indian Banks' Association
NPCI's major payment systems are UPI, RuPay, IMPS and FASTag
NPCI's headquarters is in Mumbai, Maharashtra

quizzes.passage: Unified Payments Interface (UPI) has grown into a large digital payment infrastructure that handles billions of transactions every month. As the network expands, it serves more users and more transactions, and its server capacity and customer support must keep pace. To meet these needs, the National Payments Corporation of India introduced a Merchant Discount Rate framework for certain UPI transactions. The framework gives the payment ecosystem a revenue mechanism of its own. The zero-MDR policy, introduced in 2020, had exempted merchants from paying any fee for UPI and RuPay transactions to encourage digital adoption, particularly among small traders and informal sectors. The new framework is designed so that everyday low-value transactions remain free, and the government and the payments body have both emphasised protecting small merchants and ordinary users from additional costs. Essential services such as railways, telecom, insurance and fuel are treated separately under the framework. Capital markets also receive a separate treatment. The booklet presents the framework against this background of network growth, and readers should look at its reasons as well as its rates to understand why it was introduced.

quizzes.passage: The network behind UPI handles a very large number of payments each month, and that volume keeps growing. Growth of this kind places heavy demands on the systems that run the network. Equipment and software must be upgraded regularly, and server capacity must expand as more users join. Customer support also has to be maintained for a large base of users. Fraud and other threats appear as digital payments become more common, so the operators must watch for them constantly. The Merchant Discount Rate framework was introduced to address these demands. It creates a revenue source inside the payment ecosystem. Before the framework, the zero-MDR policy had allowed merchants to accept UPI and RuPay payments without any fee, an arrangement that encouraged digital adoption among small traders and informal sectors. Under the new framework, everyday low-value transactions remain free, and the government and the National Payments Corporation of India have stressed the need to protect small merchants and ordinary users from additional costs. The framework is therefore presented as a way to sustain the network while keeping daily payments affordable for people who use them.

quizzes.passage: Unified Payments Interface, widely known as UPI, lets people send and receive money through mobile applications linked to their bank accounts. Individuals use it to pay one another, and merchants use it to accept payments at shops, restaurants and online outlets. The network has grown into a major platform that handles a very large number of transactions every month, and its services are meant for both small and large users. Many everyday low-value transactions take place on it. Behind the system is an organisation that operates and develops retail payment and settlement systems in India. Digital payments have expanded over the years, and the booklet links this growth to the need for continued investment. Keeping such a network working smoothly is a continuing task, and the booklet describes several areas that need attention as it grows. The framework discussed in the booklet applies to merchant payments above a certain value and treats some sectors separately. Readers who want to understand it should look at its slabs, its exemptions and the reasons behind it.

quizzes.passage: UPI is used for transfers between individuals and for payments made to merchants. The payments are made through mobile applications, and the network processes them quickly. One category of payments is made from a customer to a business, and the booklet explains how fees apply to such payments. The fee charged for handling a digital payment is known by a short form that appears throughout the booklet. The fee falls on the business that receives the money, while the framework for it is designed around a few value slabs. The revenue from these fees stays within the network and helps support its work. Among the countries listed as accepting the system are several in Asia, along with a small number of other nations on different continents. The network is operated by a body whose functions include developing and operating payment systems across the country. Many small businesses and informal sectors were encouraged to adopt digital payments in earlier years, when merchants paid no fee at all. The booklet presents the framework as one that fits into the wider payment ecosystem and protects ordinary users from additional costs. Readers who want to understand the framework should look at its slabs, its exemptions and the reasons behind it.
